To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the 3D structure, local structure, and atomic dynamics of Pt NPs can be strongly affected by the nature of their substrate.

the structure and shape of size-selected Pt NPS are affected by the support, and that these effects can be resolved in a quantitative fashion by combining XAFS spectroscopy with atomistic simulations and advanced XAFS analysis.

the shape of Pt NPs is affected by their interaction with the support and that Pt NPs deposited and annealed on SiO2/S1(111) are spherical, whereas NPs deposited and treated in a similar way on TiO2 assume a truncated-octahedral shape with (100) interfacial and (111) top facets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure of Pt nanocatalysts and their interactions with their environment.
a detailed characterization of the local structure of Pt NPS and its anisotropically and the effect of the support on the structure of the NPs.

understanding the role of the environment on the local structure of metal NPs, which may provide new insight into the structure–property relations of metal NPs and the role of support interactions in their catalytic properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Pt NPs deposited and annealed on TiO2 are strongly influenced by the support, whereas Pt NPs deposited onto SiO2 are not, as the support–metal interactions are much weaker.
the support has an important influence on the Pt NP structure, but it is also important to consider the influence of the ligands and adsorbates on the NP structure.
the Pt NPs are more stable in a spherical shape on SiO2, whereas they are more stable on the TiO2(1 × 1) surface as a truncated octahedral NP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of advanced XAFS analysis and atomistic simulations can provide a powerful method for the characterization of buried interfaces in supported metal NPs.
the structure and shape of Pt NPs are strongly influenced by their support.

in situ XAFs is an ideal tool to study the local atomic structure of nanoparticles, and the combination of XAFS with STM and AFM allows us to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the structure of nanoparticles on different supports.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structure of the buried interface between the NPs and the support is of paramount importance and should be taken into account in the interpretation of catalytic properties of NPs.

the support can be used to control the shape and structure of NPs and that the combination of advanced XAFS analysis techniques with STM and AFM provides a unique insight into the buried particle/support interface.

in situ XAF spectroscopy coupled with atomistic modeling can be used to gain insight into particle–support interactions that are crucial for understanding the structure of NPs and their catalytic behavior.
